proof:
Conventions. E := Ambient n ℓ = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin (n+ℓ)) = ℝ^{n+ℓ} with its Borel σ-algebra; B_s(ξ) := closedBall ξ s is the CLOSED ball, so x ∈ B_s(ξ) ⟺ |x − ξ| ≤ s (dist x ξ = |x − ξ|); r = r(x) := |x − ξ| ≥ 0; λ is Lebesgue measure on ℝ and ∫_{(a,b]} means the integral over Ioc a b; 1_S is the indicator function of S. Put B := B_R(ξ) and F_m(x) := φ_m(r(x)/t)·f(x). (Context only: Steps 3–5 of the parent proof, for a general integrable f and a general radius t; no positivity of ε_m is needed.)
1. (Vanishing off B.) Let x ∉ B, i.e. r(x) > R. For every m, (1 + ε_m)t ≤ R < r(x); dividing by t > 0 gives r(x)/t > 1 + ε_m, in particular r(x)/t ≥ 1 + ε_m, so φ_m(r(x)/t) = 0 and F_m(x) = 0.
2. (Measurability.) By 1, F_m = 1_B·F_m. The map x ↦ φ_m(r(x)/t) is Borel measurable (φ_m is measurable and x ↦ |x − ξ|/t is continuous), and f is a.e. strongly measurable for μ⌞B because f is μ-integrable on B; hence the product F_m is a.e. strongly measurable for μ⌞B. Since B is a closed, hence measurable, set, 1_B·F_m is a.e. strongly measurable for μ (aestronglyMeasurable_indicator_iff); that is, F_m is a.e. strongly measurable for μ, for every m.
3. (Domination.) Put g := 1_B·|f|. For x ∈ B, |F_m(x)| = φ_m(r(x)/t)·|f(x)| ≤ |f(x)| = g(x) because 0 ≤ φ_m ≤ 1; for x ∉ B, |F_m(x)| = 0 = g(x) by 1. So |F_m| ≤ g on E for every m. Since |f| is μ-integrable on B, g is μ-integrable (integrable_indicator_iff).
4. (Pointwise limit.) Fix x ∈ E. If x ∈ B_t(ξ) then r(x) ≤ t, so r(x)/t ≤ 1 (t > 0) and φ_m(r(x)/t) = 1 for every m; thus F_m(x) = f(x) for every m and F_m(x) → f(x) = 1_{B_t(ξ)}(x)f(x). If x ∉ B_t(ξ) then r(x) > t, so δ := r(x)/t − 1 > 0; since ε_m → 0 there is m₀ with ε_m < δ for all m ≥ m₀, i.e. r(x)/t > 1 + ε_m, hence φ_m(r(x)/t) = 0 and F_m(x) = 0 for m ≥ m₀; thus F_m(x) → 0 = 1_{B_t(ξ)}(x)f(x). Hence F_m → 1_{B_t(ξ)}·f pointwise on E.
5. (Dominated convergence.) By 2, 3 and 4, the dominated convergence theorem (tendsto_integral_filter_of_dominated_convergence with bound g and the filter atTop on ℕ) gives ∫F_m dμ → ∫1_{B_t(ξ)}·f dμ. Since B_t(ξ) is measurable, ∫1_{B_t(ξ)}·f dμ = ∫_{B_t(ξ)} f dμ (integral_indicator). This is the claim.
